planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown clumps in spring in consistently moist to wet, acidic, sandy or peaty soil in full sun; toothache grass grows naturally in seasonally wet pine flatwoods and savannas of the Gulf and Atlantic coastal plain and does poorly if the soil is allowed to dry out for extended periods.

directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, acidic, sandy or peaty soil in full sun; toothache grass is a clump-forming native bunchgrass of longleaf pine savannas and wet flatwoods from North Carolina to Texas, valued in native plant and rain-garden plantings for its strikingly unusual seed heads — narrow, one-sided, gently curved spikes that arch like a comb and turn coppery-bronze in late summer and fall, unlike the tufted or plume-like heads of most ornamental grasses. The fine-textured blue-green foliage stays low and tidy through the growing season before the flowering stems rise above it. The common name refers to the historical use of the aromatic, pungent roots, which were chewed by Native Americans and early settlers to numb toothache pain — a genuine local anesthetic effect, though the plant is grown today strictly as an ornamental and is not otherwise used medicinally. It needs consistently wet to moist, acidic soil and does not tolerate summer drought, so it is best suited to rain gardens, pond margins, and low, seasonally soggy spots rather than typical dry perennial borders. Cut back old foliage in late winter before new growth emerges.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in consistently moist to wet, acidic soil in full sun; muck sunflower grows naturally in wet pine savannas, bogs, and roadside ditches of the western Gulf coastal plain and spreads readily from divided rhizome sections.

directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, acidic, moderately fertile soil in full sun; muck sunflower is a lesser-known native perennial sunflower of the wet pine savannas, seepage bogs, and ditches of Louisiana, Texas, and Arkansas, closely resembling swamp sunflower but generally somewhat shorter and later-blooming, holding off its show of bright yellow, orange-centered daisy flowers until the very end of the season, often into November. Growing where the ground stays saturated for much of the year, it is a good choice for the wet edge of a rain garden or low spot that stays soggy after storms rather than a typical dry border, and it spreads by rhizomes into a substantial colony over a few seasons. The late, heavy bloom is an important nectar source for migrating monarch butterflies and native bees when few other flowers remain. Divide congested clumps every few years in early spring to control spread and rejuvenate flowering.
sources: Alan Weakley — Flora of the Southeastern United States
